# Cloudflare One

Before citing limits, settings, API fields, category IDs, or exact UI paths, retrieve current information from the [Cloudflare One docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/), the Cloudflare docs MCP server, or the Cloudflare API schema.

## Workflow

1. Classify the ask: architecture, configuration, troubleshooting, migration, or review.
2. Gather context: account ID, users/sites/apps, identity provider, SCIM/group sync, device management, traffic path, compliance constraints, and rollout blast radius.
3. Retrieve only the current docs needed for the products involved: Access, Gateway, WARP/device client, Tunnel/Mesh, Cloudflare WAN, DLP, CASB, device posture, or identity.
4. If account access is available, inspect existing resources before proposing or making changes: Access apps/policies/groups/IdPs, Gateway rules/lists/categories, device profiles/posture checks, tunnels/routes, DNS/resolver settings, and locations/sites.
5. Propose the change set with prerequisites, validation, and rollback. For risky changes, stage disabled or scoped to a pilot group/site unless the user explicitly asks otherwise.

## Assessment Prompts

Use these to avoid jumping straight to configuration. Ask only the prompts relevant to the user's task.

### Architecture and Current State

- Sites and users: offices, branches, data centers, VPCs, remote users, contractors, user counts, and current connectivity model.
- Applications and destinations: SaaS, public apps, private apps, APIs, infrastructure targets, protocols, ports, hostnames, and IP ranges.
- Connectivity: VPN, MPLS, SD-WAN, direct Internet breakout, centralized backhaul, site-to-site needs, and private DNS architecture.
- Security stack: current SWG, NGFW, VPN/ZTNA, DLP, CASB, email security, logging, and compliance requirements.
- Identity: IdP, SCIM/group sync, group naming, multi-IdP needs, service accounts, and contractor/partner access.
- Rollout: pilot users/sites, blast radius, rollback path, support owners, and success criteria.

### Access and SaaS Federation

- App shape: web app, API, SSH/RDP/VNC, database, SaaS app, public hostname, private IP, or private hostname. Retrieve [Access application type](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/choose-application-type/) docs before choosing.
- Access model: clientless browser access, private networking with device client, peer to peer connectivity, service connections with service tokens or mutual TLS, or SaaS SSO federation.
- Policy needs: user groups, device posture, session duration, mTLS, service tokens, and app launcher visibility. Retrieve [Access policy](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/policies/) docs before configuring selectors or evaluation order.
- SaaS details: SAML vs OIDC support, ACS/redirect URLs, Entity IDs/client IDs, required attributes, and tenant-control requirements.

### Tunnel and Private Networking

- Sites and segments: which data centers, VPCs, offices, or network segments need connectivity.
- HA: dev/test single connector, production multiple connectors, or advanced multi-tunnel/site redundancy.
- Runtime: where cloudflared or WARP Connector/Mesh will run: VM, container, Kubernetes, bare metal, or other target.
- Egress: whether connectors can reach Cloudflare over the required outbound ports/protocols. Retrieve [Tunnel connectivity prechecks](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/troubleshoot-tunnels/connectivity-prechecks/) before naming exact endpoints.
- Origin reachability: whether the connector can resolve and reach every private origin.
- Routing: required CIDRs/hostnames, overlapping IP spaces, [virtual networks](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/private-net/cloudflared/tunnel-virtual-networks/), [Split Tunnels](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/team-and-resources/devices/cloudflare-one-client/configure/route-traffic/split-tunnels/), and private DNS/[resolver policy](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/traffic-policies/resolver-policies/) needs.
- Management model: prefer remotely managed/token-based tunnels for new deployments unless there is a clear reason for local config.

### Gateway, TLS, and DLP

- Traffic controls: DNS categories, HTTP URL/path inspection, L4 ports/protocols, egress IP requirements, custom lists, and allow/block exceptions. Retrieve [Gateway traffic policy](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/traffic-policies/) docs for current selectors and order of enforcement.
- Identity: whether Gateway policies need user or group selectors, and whether users will be authenticated through WARP/IdP context. Check [Gateway identity selectors](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/traffic-policies/identity-selectors/) and [SCIM provisioning](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/team-and-resources/users/scim/) when groups are involved.
- TLS inspection: root CA deployment path, certificate-pinned applications, compliance exceptions, and FIPS requirements. Retrieve [TLS decryption](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/traffic-policies/http-policies/tls-decryption/) docs before enabling.
- DLP: sensitive data types, channels to inspect, TLS inspection readiness, DLP profiles, payload logging requirements, and false-positive tolerance. Retrieve [DLP](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/data-loss-prevention/) docs before creating enforcement.

### CASB, Device Posture, and Risk

- CASB: SaaS vendors, admin access level, scan policy, org size, remediation owner, and whether inline protection is also required. Retrieve [CASB findings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/cloud-and-saas-findings/manage-findings/) docs before recommending remediation.
- Device posture: required checks, third-party EDR/MDM integrations, enrollment rules, device profiles, and split tunnel alignment.
- Risk scoring: relevant behavior signals, false-positive sources such as VPNs or service accounts, and whether risk is for investigation or enforcement. Retrieve [user risk score](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/team-and-resources/users/risk-score/) docs before using risk in policies.

### Cloudflare WAN / Site Connectivity

- Site topology, on-ramp type, route ownership, tunnel redundancy, static vs BGP-managed routes, network firewall needs, and appliance/profile ownership. Retrieve [Cloudflare WAN](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-wan/) and [Cloudflare Network Firewall](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-network-firewall/) docs before proposing site connectivity changes.

## Guardrails

- Access controls application authorization; Gateway controls traffic inspection/filtering. Use both when the requirement spans identity-aware app access and network/web security.
- For new Access deployments, create policies through the reusable policy API (`/access/policies`) and attach them to applications. Do not send inline `policies` in an application create/update request unless the current API documentation explicitly requires an app-scoped policy.
- Treat an app-scoped policy reported as `reusable: false` as legacy. Migrate existing policies with the documented `make_reusable` endpoint or replace them with reusable policies; do not create new legacy policies. Distinguish legacy policies from the deprecated legacy private-network application type.
- Public hostname Access apps can be clientless. Private destination apps require WARP/Device client or another network on-ramp plus routes and DNS resolution. Retrieve [self-hosted private app](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/non-http/self-hosted-private-app/) docs before configuring private destinations.
- Cloudflare Tunnel is an off-ramp from a private network to Cloudflare. Cloudflare WAN and Mesh are other off-ramps which can also be on-ramps.
- Group-based policies depend on IdP group claims or SCIM. If group sync is missing, do not invent group selectors.
- Private hostnames need explicit DNS routing/resolution; creating an Access app alone is not enough. Use [resolver policies](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/traffic-policies/resolver-policies/) and review [Connect a private hostname](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/private-net/cloudflared/connect-private-hostname/)
- HTTP inspection and DLP for encrypted web traffic require TLS inspection and planned Do Not Inspect exceptions.
- Gateway DNS, Network, HTTP, and Egress policies have different evaluation semantics. Retrieve [order of enforcement](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/traffic-policies/order-of-enforcement/) docs before explaining precedence.
- Start broad block/allow/DLP/TLS policies disabled limited to a pilot with specific target users or groups unless the user approves a wider rollout.

### Identity and Access

- Access Groups are Cloudflare objects; IdP/SCIM groups are identity claims. Gateway group selectors use synced IdP groups, not Access Groups.
- Group names and SAML/OIDC attributes are case-sensitive. Verify exact claim names and values before creating group-based rules.
- SCIM changes and group membership can be stale until sync and re-authentication complete. Troubleshoot with the user's last authenticated identity, not just the IdP state.
- Access policies are default-deny. A private app with routes but no Allow policy still blocks access.
- Access policy selectors can use IP lists, not Gateway domain or URL lists.
- SaaS federation handles authentication into the SaaS app. SaaS authorization and tenant restrictions usually require SaaS-side roles and/or Gateway tenant controls.
- Browser Rendering for SSH/VNC/RDP is an Access capability. Browser Isolation renders general web content remotely. Do not conflate them.

### Device Client Deployment

- The [Cloudflare One device client](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/team-and-resources/devices/cloudflare-one-client/) is the on-ramp for user devices. Two components control it: **enrollment rules** (who can connect) and **device profiles** (how the client behaves after enrollment).
- The enrollment rule is an Access application of type `warp`, not a device setting. It accepts reusable Access policies. Look in Access for enrollment debugging, not Devices.
- For headless or autonomous devices (services, kiosks, Linux hosts), use service token enrollment. Non-human devices authenticate as `non_identity@[team-domain].cloudflareaccess.com` and have no group membership - device profiles targeting IdP groups will not match them. Target headless devices explicitly with the non-identity email, specific conventions about the devices (OS information, etc.),or let them fall to the default profile.
- Device profiles control connection mode, [split tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/team-and-resources/devices/cloudflare-one-client/configure/route-traffic/split-tunnels/) configuration, user permissions (disable, switch lock), auto-reconnect, and captive portal behavior. Profiles are matched by user group or device attributes in precedence order - first match wins, default profile catches the rest.
- Split tunnel mode is the single most impactful client setting. Choose the mode based on the deployment goal:

  | Goal | Mode | Rationale |
  |---|---|---|
  | VPN replacement only (private apps) | **Include** | Route only specified private CIDRs and hostnames through the client. Everything else goes direct. Minimal blast radius. |
  | SWG only (internet security) | **Exclude** | All traffic through the client. Exclude only what breaks (local printers, certificate-pinned apps). |
  | VPN replacement + SWG | **Exclude** | All traffic through the client. Most common enterprise configuration. |
  | Coexistence with another VPN | **Include** | Avoids conflict with the other VPN's tunnel interface and DNS control. |
  | DNS filtering only | DNS-only mode | Only DNS queries go to Gateway. No traffic proxying. |

- Include vs exclude is per-profile, not per-entry. You cannot mix modes in the same profile. Switching modes mid-deployment requires re-evaluating every entry.
- Split tunnel entries must align with tunnel routes bidirectionally. A CIDR in the include list without a matching tunnel route causes a black hole. A tunnel route without a matching device profile entry means traffic never enters the tunnel.
- MDM parameters (`mdm.xml` / managed preferences) override dashboard-configured profile settings for any setting specified in the file. If dashboard changes appear to have no effect on managed devices, check MDM config. Retrieve [MDM deployment](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/team-and-resources/devices/cloudflare-one-client/deployment/mdm-deployment/) docs for platform-specific file locations and parameters.
- If another VPN client or agent controls DNS on the device, the device client's DNS interception will conflict. In coexistence scenarios, use "traffic only" mode to avoid routing table and DNS conflicts.
- Captive portal detection temporarily disconnects the client when it detects a portal (hotel WiFi, airport).  This is a common source of end-user friction and should be managed carefully.

### Private Networking

- Split tunnel mode changes the meaning of every route decision: Exclude mode sends traffic to Cloudflare when removed from excludes; Include mode sends traffic only when added to includes.
- Virtual networks should be used primarily when IP subnets overlap and hostname-based routing is not used. It can be used to control other user connectivity behavior, but it is recommended to manage through security policies.
- A healthy tunnel only proves cloudflared can reach Cloudflare. The tunnel must have appropriate published application routes, network routes, or hostname routes for connectivity to function.
- Cloudflare Tunnel and Cloudflare Mesh can both be used to facilitate connectivity to internal networks. Cloudflare WAN can as well, but it is gated behind Enterprise subscriptions. Retrieve [choose an on-ramp](https://developers.cloudflare.com/learning-paths/secure-internet-traffic/connect-devices-networks/choose-on-ramp/) when deliberating between Tunnel types.
- Run multiple cloudflared connectors for production HA, preferably on separate hosts. Token-based, remotely managed tunnels are the default for new deployments.

### Gateway, TLS, and DLP

- `dns.domains` matches a domain and subdomains; `dns.fqdn` is exact-match only.
- DNS pre-resolution selectors and post-resolution selectors do not behave like a single strict precedence list. Retrieve current evaluation docs before changing rule order.
- HTTP Do Not Inspect rules run before HTTP Allow/Block/Isolate behavior. A later block rule will not override an earlier inspection bypass.
- Certificate-pinned apps need Do Not Inspect exceptions before broad TLS inspection. Deploy the Cloudflare root CA to managed devices before enabling inspection.
- DLP profiles are detection definitions only. They do nothing until referenced by Gateway HTTP policies or CASB scan settings. Rules with body inspection may be evaluated multiple times in a single pass.
- Start DLP with payload logging where appropriate, tune false positives, then block.
- Gateway Network policies are strict L4 controls. Identity-aware L4 matching requires authenticated device context.

### CASB, Risk, and Operations

- API CASB is out-of-band and periodic. It does not provide real-time inline enforcement although some integrations support "remediation"; use Gateway granular application controls for inline CASB capability for supported applications. Retrieve [Granular application controls](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/traffic-policies/http-policies/granular-controls/) when creating security policies for specific actions in specific SaaS applications.
- CASB findings are tied to specific assets and instances. Drill into affected assets before recommending remediation.
- Use current Dashboard remediation guidance for CASB fixes. Most remediations happen in the SaaS admin console, not Cloudflare.
- Large SaaS integrations can take 24-48 hours for initial scans. Reauthorizing can restart scan state; check credential health before reconnecting.
- User risk scores are behavior-based and asynchronous. CASB findings do not automatically imply high user risk.

### Infrastructure Access

- [Zero Trust Infrastructure Access](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/non-http/infrastructure-apps/) (ZTIA) is the purpose-built offering for SSH access through the device client. It provides capabilities not available through self-hosted apps: keystroke logging, control over how users authenticate to the target machine, [short-lived certificates](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/use-cases/ssh/ssh-infrastructure-access/#generate-a-cloudflare-ssh-ca) that replace static SSH keys with ephemeral certs tied to Access identity, and lightweight privileged access management. Use Infrastructure Access apps for SSH when the device client is deployed.
- [Browser Rendering](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/non-http/browser-rendering/) provides clientless SSH, RDP, and VNC through the browser without requiring the device client. Clientless RDP includes session recording and file transfer controls. Use clientless access when a device client cannot be installed (contractors, partner access, unmanaged devices) - typically not as the default for managed users with the client installed.
- [Audit SSH](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/use-cases/ssh/ssh-infrastructure-access/#enable-ssh-command-logging) is a Gateway Network policy action that logs SSH commands without blocking. It requires the session to be proxied through Cloudflare.
- Short-lived certificates require CA configuration on the target host and `sshd` configured to trust the Cloudflare CA public key. Retrieve [short-lived certificate setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/identity/users/short-lived-certificates/) docs before configuring.
- For kubectl and database access behind private networks, use the device client with private destination routing. There is no Infrastructure Access or browser-rendered equivalent for arbitrary TCP protocols today.

### Logs, Analytics, and DEX

- [Gateway activity logs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/analytics/logs/gateway-logs/) record DNS, HTTP, and Network policy decisions. Filter by rule name, user identity, destination, action, and time range. These are the primary troubleshooting tool for "why was this blocked/allowed."
- [Access audit logs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/insights/logs/dashboard-logs/access-authentication-logs/) record authentication decisions per app - who authenticated, which policy matched, and session details. Use for verifying policy behavior and investigating access failures.
- [Shadow IT discovery](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/insights/analytics/shadow-it-discovery/) uses Gateway HTTP logs to surface unmanaged SaaS applications. Requires TLS inspection for HTTPS visibility.
- [DEX (Digital Experience Monitoring)](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/insights/dex/) provides fleet-level and per-device connectivity diagnostics. Use [DEX tests](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/insights/dex/tests/) (HTTP, traceroute) to proactively monitor reachability to critical origins and internal apps. Fleet status shows device client health, connection mode, and connectivity state across the enrolled population.
- [Logpush](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/analytics/logs/logpush/) exports Gateway, Access, Network, and DEX logs to external SIEM or storage. Configure before go-live if the customer requires centralized log retention or compliance reporting.
- When troubleshooting, work from logs toward config: identify the log entry showing the failure (Gateway block, Access deny, tunnel error, DNS resolution miss), then trace back to the responsible rule, route, or policy.

### Cloudflare WAN / Site Connectivity

- Cloudflare WAN is connectivity, not a security service. Apply inspection and policy with Gateway and Network Firewall where required.
- WAN firewall expressions are not the same language as Gateway wirefilter expressions. Retrieve the current syntax before editing.
- Generated IPsec PSKs and some OAuth/client secrets are returned once. Store them immediately.

## Output Defaults

- Designs: current assumptions, target architecture, product responsibilities, rollout phases, validation, and open decisions.
- Configuration work: prerequisites, exact resources to inspect/create/change, test cases, and rollback.
- Troubleshooting: traffic path, likely failure point, evidence to collect, and next test.

## Validation Prompts

- Access: test authorized, unauthorized, posture-failing, service-token, and multi-IdP flows when applicable; inspect logs and policy precedence. For new policies, verify they are managed through the reusable policy collection and not returned as `reusable: false` app-scoped policies.
- Private network access: verify route lookup, tunnel health, origin reachability, split tunnel behavior, DNS resolution, and end-to-end access from a device client test device.
- Gateway: verify rule type, action, traffic expression, precedence/evaluation phase, referenced lists, and Gateway settings before enabling broadly.
- TLS/DLP: test Do Not Inspect exceptions and root CA trust before enabling inspection; test DLP with known samples and monitor false positives before blocking.
- CASB/risk: confirm integration health, credential expiry, asset discovery, scan timing, finding instances, and risk-score signal latency before declaring remediation complete.
- Cloudflare WAN: verify tunnel health, route priority/ownership, traffic flow, firewall expression syntax, and connector/appliance telemetry where applicable.

## API Safety

- Use fully qualified MCP tool names when MCP tools are available.
- Never guess category IDs, application IDs, wirefilter fields, or API request bodies. Retrieve the current schema/docs and existing account objects.
- Do not enable broad production policies without explicit approval.

=== infra/README
# Infra

Terraform for Kip's server: a Vultr instance in London behind Caddy, its firewall, a private
container registry, and the MongoDB Atlas access entry for the instance's IP. Tiger Cloud is
passed in as a URI. Architecture and the deploy flow: `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` ("Deploy").

## What it creates
| Resource | Notes |
|---|---|
| `vultr_ssh_key.team` | From `ssh_public_key_path` (default `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`) |
| `vultr_container_registry.kip` | Private, plan `start_up`, in `region` |
| `vultr_firewall_group.api` + rules | 22 from `admin_ip` only; 80 and 443 open for Caddy |
| `vultr_reserved_ip.api` | Fixed IPv4, so the API URL survives `-replace` |
| `vultr_instance.api` | `vc2-2c-4gb`, Ubuntu 24.04 (`os_id` 2284), in `lhr`, on the reserved IP |
| `mongodbatlas_project_ip_access_list.api` | Allows the instance's IP into Atlas |

`cloud-init.yaml.tftpl` installs Docker, writes `/opt/kip/.env`, a Caddyfile and a compose file,
derives `<ip>.sslip.io` from instance metadata, logs in to the registry and starts the API, the
worker and Caddy. Outputs: `api_ip`, `api_url`, `registry_urn`.

## First apply
1. Credentials in your shell (from 1Password or the MLH emails, never committed):
   `VULTR_API_KEY`, `MONGODB_ATLAS_PUBLIC_KEY`, `MONGODB_ATLAS_PRIVATE_KEY`.
2. `cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars` and fill it in (git-ignored).
3. Create the registry first, then push the image to it:
   ```bash
   terraform -chdir=infra init
   terraform -chdir=infra apply -target=vultr_container_registry.kip
   ```

# Decisions

Append-only log, newest at the bottom. Add an entry when a choice would surprise a newcomer or is
costly to undo. Agents also record it with `entire brain remember "<decision>"`.

Format:

```
## YYYY-MM-DD: <decision>
**Context:** why it came up.
**Decision:** what we chose.
**Consequences:** what follows, good and bad.
```

## 2026-11-13: GitHub Issues is the single task queue
**Context:** Up to ~10 agents across Claude Code, Codex and Cursor need one shared view of the
work. A second tracker (beads, Backlog.md, Task Master) would drift from GitHub.
**Decision:** Every task is a GitHub issue in the task form. `./hq` claims, labels and ships them.
Humans dispatch; agents never pick their own.
**Consequences:** GitHub is the only shared state; `.context/` and workspaces are scratch. Every
agent needs `gh` auth and network access.

## 2026-11-13: Entire for sessions, memory and review
**Context:** We want shared session history, codebase mapping, persistent memory and cross-vendor
review, and we target Best Use of Entire. Entire's judging tool only reads `refs/heads/entire/*`.
**Decision:** Use Entire Sessions, Graph, Brain and Trails, and `entire review` (Claude Code and
Codex reviewers, one judge). Use the `branch` checkpoint backend.
**Consequences:** Every session is recorded and pushed, so no secrets in prompts. Each clone runs
`entire enable`. `review:pass` needs local `entire review`, hosted Trail review or `/hq-review`.

## 2026-11-13: Squash merges keep Entire-Checkpoint trailers
**Context:** Entire links commits to sessions through `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers. A squash
message without them breaks the link.
**Decision:** Squash merge only. Repo setting: squash title = PR title, message = commit details.
`./hq ship` merges this way.
**Consequences:** `main` gets one commit per PR and `entire why` still resolves to sessions. Never
edit the trailers out of a squash message.

## 2026-11-13: Fresh submission repo from this template at kick-off
**Context:** MLH only judges work done during the event, and Entire's judging tool scores a clean
start higher.
**Decision:** This repo is a template. At kick-off we run `gh repo create --template` and hack in
the new repo.
**Consequences:** The submission has no pre-event history. Pre-kick-off agent sessions are closed
and fresh ones started. The README discloses the framework as pre-event tooling.

## 2026-11-14: Kip is the project
**Context:** The plan "Kip: Sleep, Noise and the City" (Nick, 2026-11-14) covers product, business
model, stack, build plan and pitch.
**Decision:** Build Kip. Product in `docs/SPEC.md`, business in `docs/BUSINESS.md`, science and
wording rules in `docs/DOMAIN.md`, stack and contracts in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`.
**Consequences:** Every agent follows `docs/DOMAIN.md` for anything it computes or shows.

## 2026-11-14: The API is the only caller of third-party services
**Context:** Gemini, ElevenLabs and Solana need secret keys; the app (iOS and web) is a client.
**Decision:** Only the API calls Gemini, ElevenLabs and Solana. Clients call the API.
**Consequences:** Keys live in one place. Clip labelling and briefings need a network round trip.

## 2026-11-14: Tiger for time series, MongoDB for documents and geo
**Context:** Kip has dense timestamped data (1 Hz noise, sensor readings, vitals) and geo
documents (hotels, sensors, works). Both are sponsor tracks.
**Decision:** Every timestamped value goes in Tiger; MongoDB holds users, one summary per night,
hotels, sensors, works, venues and scores. If the event limits us to one sponsor track, enter
MongoDB: move the time series into MongoDB time series collections and make hotel ranking the
centrepiece.
**Consequences:** Two stores to provision and delete from. User deletion must cover both.

## 2026-11-14: Read Watch data through HealthKit, not a Watch app
**Context:** An all-night workout session drains 40% to 100% of a Watch battery, and Watch app
signing is a known time sink.
**Decision:** The iPhone reads the Watch's own sleep tracking from HealthKit after the night ends.
A watchOS app is a stretch, abandoned if signing doesn't work by hour 2.
**Consequences:** Sleep stages arrive only after the session ends, so the live demo uses the
phone alone.

## 2026-11-14: Claim links, not causes; label estimates
**Context:** One night has 2 to 6 wake-ups, phone dB is uncalibrated, and the WHO curve is for
long-term road traffic at the facade, not kerbside sensors.
**Decision:** Show counts against a random-window baseline, relative dB, and an "indicative" city
map. Follow the wording table in `docs/DOMAIN.md`.
**Consequences:** Weaker-sounding claims that survive judge questions.

## 2026-11-14: Placeholder booking links for the demo
**Context:** Affiliate approval takes weeks; Booking.com cut small affiliates in 2025.
**Decision:** Hotels come from OpenStreetMap with placeholder booking links. Apply to a network
anyway and don't quote a commission rate until confirmed.
**Consequences:** Revenue is shown as the model, not as live bookings.

## 2026-11-14: Solana mainnet with the Memo program only
**Context:** We want cheap public timestamps a council can check without trusting Kip.
**Decision:** Hash each night's log and write it to mainnet with the Memo program. No Anchor, no
custom program.
**Consequences:** No toolchain setup; a fraction of a penny per night. It proves when a log
existed, not that it's true, and we say so.

## 2026-11-14: Bun workspaces; one server package and image
**Context:** The API and worker share clients, schemas and database code, and the plan wants one
Docker image.
**Decision:** Bun is the package manager for the whole repo and the server runtime.
`apps/server` holds both entrypoints (`main.api.ts`, `main.worker.ts`) and builds with the Expo
web export into one image.
**Consequences:** One build and deploy, one lockfile. Never hand-merge `bun.lock`.

## 2026-11-14: React Native on Expo for both the phone and the dashboard
**Context:** The team's strongest language is TypeScript, and the demo needs an iPhone app and a
browser dashboard.
**Decision:** One Expo app (dev client, Expo Router) builds iOS and web. HealthKit through
`@kingstinct/react-native-healthkit`; background metering, spike clips and the speech check in a
small local Expo Module (`kip-audio`, Swift). Replaces the plan's SwiftUI app and React/Vite
dashboard.
**Consequences:** One UI codebase and shared types. The native audio module is the riskiest
piece: build and test it on a device first. Maps need a `.native`/`.web` split. A watchOS app
becomes a separate native target, so it stays a stretch.

## 2026-11-14: tRPC on Hono for the API
**Context:** App and server are both TypeScript, and several agents change API shapes in parallel.
**Decision:** tRPC v11 mounted on Hono. Every JSON call and the live subscription go through
tRPC; plain Hono routes only for binary clip upload, the Street Manager SNS endpoint, health and
the web build.
**Consequences:** End-to-end types with no codegen; a server change that breaks the app fails
typecheck. Non-TypeScript clients (SNS) still get plain HTTP.

## 2026-11-14: File tree by feature, then by layer
**Context:** Up to ~10 agents work at once. A layer-first tree (`routes/`, `services/`,
`screens/`) puts every task in the same folders.
**Decision:** Each feature (`city`, `night`, `attribution`, `labels`, `briefing`, `evidence`,
`stays`, `works`, `live`, `account`) owns a folder in `apps/mobile/src/features/`,
`apps/server/src/features/` and `packages/shared/src/`. Lanes are features. Registries are
written once in M0 with every feature stubbed; shared code changes through `platform` issues.
**Consequences:** Parallel issues touch disjoint paths. Cross-feature calls go through a feature's
`index.ts`. The rules are in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`.

## 2026-11-14: Both of us own everything
**Context:** The template gave Ellis `main`, deploys and the freeze, and gave each human lanes.
With two people working across the whole stack, that split only adds hand-offs.
**Decision:** No split ownership. Either of us can merge any PR, deploy, call the freeze and tag
`demo-v1`. Lanes stay, but only to keep parallel agents on disjoint paths.
**Consequences:** No waiting on a specific person. Say in chat before merging contracts, deploy
config or anything after the freeze, so we don't both do it.

## 2026-11-14: Train our own handling-noise filter on a Lium GPU pod
**Context:** A phone on a nightstand, in a pocket or under a pillow picks up its own handling noise
(sleeve, pocket, bedsheet rustle). Those spikes would be labelled and linked to wake-ups. We also
want a model of our own in the pipeline, not only third-party APIs.
**Decision:** Train a small PyTorch mask model on synthetic mixtures of handling noise and night
sounds, on a Lium GPU pod (Vultr stays for deployment). Export it to ONNX and run it in the API on
each spike clip before Gemini. Mostly-handling clips get the label `handling`. Clips are 16 kHz mono
WAV. Prototype quality is acceptable: if the model underperforms, the API falls back to labelling
the original clip.
**Consequences:** A Python toolchain (`uv`) beside Bun, outside `./hq check`. Training data and
checkpoints stay out of git; only the exported model is committed. The label set gains `handling`,
which attribution and briefings ignore.

## 2026-11-14: Commit a small curated audio library in `ml/audio/`
**Context:** Both of us, and agents on any machine or a Lium pod, need the same recordings and
downloaded clips, and Ellis wants to upload recordings straight into the repo.
**Decision:** `ml/audio/` holds our recordings, ESC-50 background clips, placeholder synthetic
handling noise and ElevenLabs-generated clips, all 16 kHz mono WAV with sources in
`ml/audio/SOURCES.md`, committed to git. Keep it small (tens of MB): short takes only. Generated
mixtures, runs and checkpoints still stay out of git. No Git LFS, because its hooks clash with
Entire's.
**Consequences:** Every clone carries the audio library. ESC-50 is CC BY-NC, acceptable for the
prototype only. Raw Voice Memos files stay in the ignored `ml/audio/inbox/`.

## 2026-11-14: Recordings with other people's conversation stay out of git
**Context:** The venue is loud. The room tone and the Watch's general audio are mostly other attendees
talking, and the repo becomes public at submission.
**Decision:** Every recording is scanned with Apple's sound classifier. Speech windows (confidence 0.5
or more) are cut from committed clips; recordings that are mostly conversation go to the git-ignored
`ml/audio/private/`, used for training on our machines or the Lium pod only, and deleted after the event.
**Consequences:** The committed handling set is smaller (about 3 minutes). The data pipeline must cope
with room tone being absent on a fresh clone, for example by taking the noise floor from each take's
quiet start and end.

## 2026-11-14: Web maps use Mapbox GL JS
**Context:** The web dashboard needs a basemap that stays readable under city, works and stay
layers, with selection, clustering and camera changes. The first shell used MapLibre and
OpenStreetMap raster tiles on both web and iOS.
**Decision:** `Map.web.tsx` renders with Mapbox GL JS and the restrained `light-v11` style. The
public token comes from `EXPO_PUBLIC_MAPBOX_TOKEN` (a `pk.` token, URL-restricted in the Mapbox
console, never committed). Feature code draws GeoJSON points, lines and polygons through `lib/map`
and does not import Mapbox or MapLibre. iOS stays on MapLibre with OpenStreetMap raster tiles until
a native Mapbox migration. Observatory, Street Manager and OpenStreetMap remain Kip's data sources;
the basemap is only the canvas. The map does not request device location to show Newcastle, and
Mapbox attribution stays visible.
**Consequences:** The web export shows Newcastle tiles only when the public token is set. A missing
token shows a message naming `EXPO_PUBLIC_MAPBOX_TOKEN` instead of a blank map. The phone build does
not gain a Mapbox native SDK. Secret Mapbox tokens (`sk.`) stay out of the app.

## 2026-11-14: Open questions answered: no home sensor, one sponsor track
**Context:** Two open questions in `docs/SPEC.md` changed the plan. The human answered both.
**Decision:** Nobody sleeps at home in Newcastle near an Observatory noise sensor during the event,
so the city map uses sensors near the venue and demo step 4 uses a night exported from HealthKit
(the SPEC's stated fallback). Each team is limited to one sponsor track, so we enter MongoDB per
"Tiger for time series, MongoDB for documents and geo". Still open: the event length and start
time, and what the "35" in the team's notes means. Both keep their assumptions in `docs/SPEC.md`.
**Consequences:** Follow the MongoDB fallback in that entry. Do not build on the "35".
=== README
# DurHack 2026 agent framework (template)

A small framework for running many coding agents at once during a hackathon. Claude Code, Codex
and Cursor follow the same rules. GitHub Issues is the task queue, `./hq` is the CLI around it,
and [Entire](https://entire.com) records sessions, maps the codebase, keeps memory and runs reviews.

## Pre-event tooling disclosure
This repository is a template prepared before DurHack 2026. It holds tooling, agent rules, docs
and GitHub templates only: no product code. At kick-off we create a fresh submission repo from
this template (`gh repo create --template`). All product code is written during DurHack, in that
repo.

## Quickstart
- Humans: [docs/PLAYBOOK.md](docs/PLAYBOOK.md) (kick-off checklist, dispatching agents, onboarding).
- Agents: [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) and the skills in [.agents/skills](.agents/skills).
- Hack context: [docs/hack/BRIEF.md](docs/hack/BRIEF.md), [docs/SPEC.md](docs/SPEC.md),
  [docs/BUSINESS.md](docs/BUSINESS.md), [docs/DOMAIN.md](docs/DOMAIN.md),
  [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md), [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md).
- First run in a clone: `entire enable`, then `./hq setup` (Windows: `hq.cmd setup`), then
  `./hq board`.

## Running the project
Kip is a Bun monorepo: an Expo app (`apps/mobile`, iOS and web), a Hono + tRPC server
(`apps/server`, API and worker) and shared domain code (`packages/shared`). Details in
[docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md).

```bash
bun install
cp .env.example .env        # local defaults; never commit .env
bun run db:up               # TimescaleDB + MongoDB in Docker
bun run dev:api             # http://localhost:3000; migrates on boot, skips any database not configured
bun run dev:worker          # cron jobs
bun run dev:app             # Expo: press w for web, or use a dev-client build on iPhone
./hq check                  # lint, typecheck, tests (what CI runs)
```

The iPhone app needs a dev-client build (`cd apps/mobile && bun run ios`) because of its native
modules; Expo Go won't load it. Deploy: `infra/` (Terraform) and the `Dockerfile`, see
[docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md#deploy).

# One origin for the web app and the API, so the browser never makes a cross-origin
# call. TLS ends at Cloudflare; inside the box this is plain HTTP on :80.
:80 {
	encode zstd gzip

		Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains"
		X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
		Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
		-Server

	# The API, its OpenAPI schema (what Grok Bot imports) and its docs.

	}

		reverse_proxy web:3000
	}

	# instead of a bare 502.
	handle_errors 502 {
		respond "Eden Matrix: the web app isn't deployed yet. The API is live at /v1 (docs at /docs)." 502

# Production topology. The bot publishes no ports of its own — it only dials
# out to Discord. Game servers are NOT services in this file: the bot creates
# them as sibling containers through the mounted Docker socket, labelled
# `host-node.managed=true`, with host ports drawn from HOSTNODE_PORT_RANGE.
#
# The image comes from GHCR (pushed by CI); the `build` key exists so the same
# file works locally with compose.local.yml.
name: host-node

services:
  bot:
    image: ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER:-local}/host-node-bot:${IMAGE_TAG:-latest}
    build:
      context: ..
      dockerfile: docker/bot.Dockerfile
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Secrets come from the env file only. Listing them under `environment:`
    # as well would silently win over it and blank out anything unset in the
    # shell — so infrastructure wiring lives here, credentials do not.
    env_file:
      - path: ../.env
        required: false
    environment:
      ENVIRONMENT: production
      # The only credentials stored on the server. Everything else (Discord
      # token, role ids) is fetched with them at startup and never touches
      # disk.
      INFISICAL_CLIENT_ID: ${INFISICAL_CLIENT_ID:-}
      INFISICAL_CLIENT_SECRET: ${INFISICAL_CLIENT_SECRET:-}
      INFISICAL_PROJECT_ID: ${INFISICAL_PROJECT_ID:-}
      INFISICAL_ENV: ${INFISICAL_ENV:-prod}
      # The VIP directory. Game servers keep their state in Docker; this is
      # the only thing the bot itself has to persist, so it lives on a named
      # volume that redeploys do not touch.
      HOSTNODE_DB_PATH: /data/hostnode.db
      # The status page listens here inside the container only. cloudflared
      # reaches it over the compose network, so no host port is published and
      # the box's firewall is untouched.
      HOSTNODE_WEB_PORT: "8080"
      HOSTNODE_WEB_TITLE: ${HOSTNODE_WEB_TITLE:-Oretary Servers}
    volumes:
      # The whole point of the bot — it manages the host's Docker daemon.
      # Socket access is root-equivalent on the host, which is also why the
      # container does not bother dropping to an unprivileged user: the
      # boundary that matters is who can talk to the bot, enforced in Discord.
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      - hostnode_data:/data

  # Public ingress for the status page. A separate service rather than a
  # published port: the tunnel dials out, so nothing is exposed on the host
  # and there is no certificate to renew. Unlike the game-server DNS records,
  # proxying is correct here — this genuinely is HTTP.

    image: cloudflare/cloudflared:2026.10.7
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: tunnel --no-autoupdate run
    environment:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs on the VPS, from /opt/firealarm-budget, after CI has copied the compose files and a
# freshly rendered .env.new. Touches only this project: the box is shared with other stacks.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

tag=${1:?usage: remote-deploy.sh <image tag>}

# The new settings replace the old ones in one step, readable by deploy only.
install -m 600 .env.new .env
rm -f .env.new

files=(-f deploy/compose.yml -f deploy/compose.tunnel.yml)
if grep -q "^WEB_ENABLED='true'$" .env; then
  files+=(-f deploy/compose.web.yml)
fi
compose=(docker compose --env-file .env "${files[@]}")

# Remove this project's superseded image tags *before* pulling, because the pull is what
# runs out of disk (the disk hit 100% on 2026-09-15 from other stacks' old tags).
# Scoped to our own images on purpose: other stacks run images that exist in no registry.
# `latest` and the tag being deployed are kept; rmi refuses images a container still uses.
docker images --filter 'reference=ghcr.io/ehewes/firealarm-budget-*' \
  --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}' \
  | grep -v ':latest$' | grep -v ":${tag}$" \
  | xargs -r -n1 docker rmi 2>/dev/null || true
df -h / | tail -1

"${compose[@]}" pull
"${compose[@]}" up -d --remove-orphans

# The Caddyfile is a bind mount, and changing it does not recreate the container.
"${compose[@]}" exec -T caddy caddy reload --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile --adapter caddyfile \
  || echo "caddy reload skipped (container was just recreated)"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Post-deploy checks, run on the VPS from inside the containers, never through the tunnel
# (a tunnel or Cloudflare problem is not a failed release, and vice versa).
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

files=(-f deploy/compose.yml -f deploy/compose.tunnel.yml)
web=false
if grep -q "^WEB_ENABLED='true'$" .env; then
  files+=(-f deploy/compose.web.yml)
  web=true
fi
compose=(docker compose --env-file .env "${files[@]}")

fail() {
  echo "SMOKE FAILED: $1" >&2
  "${compose[@]}" ps
  "${compose[@]}" logs --tail=80 "${2:-api}"
  exit 1
}

ready=false
for _ in $(seq 1 40); do
  if "${compose[@]}" exec -T api python -c \
    "import urllib.request;urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/ready')" 2> /dev/null; then
    ready=true
    break
  fi
  sleep 3
done
[ "$ready" = true ] || fail "the API never became ready (database unreachable?)"

"${compose[@]}" exec -T caddy wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1/v1/health > /dev/null \
  || fail "Caddy does not route /v1 to the API" caddy
if [ "$web" = true ]; then
  "${compose[@]}" exec -T caddy wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1/ > /dev/null \
    || fail "Caddy does not reach the web app" web
fi

not_running=$("${compose[@]}" ps --format '{{.Service}} {{.State}}' | awk '$2 != "running"')
[ -z "$not_running" ] || fail "not running: $not_running" cloudflared

echo "smoke OK: api ready, caddy routing, all services running"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Ships a commit to the Docker host and restarts Kip behind its Cloudflare tunnel:
#   infra/tunnel/deploy.sh [git ref]    (default HEAD; DEPLOY_HOST overrides the ssh host)
# Only committed files ship (git archive). The image is built on the host, which is amd64,
# so there is no registry and no cross-build. Secrets stay in /opt/kip/.env on the host.
set -euo pipefail

ref=${1:-HEAD}
host=${DEPLOY_HOST:-ehewesagents}
url=${KIP_URL:-https://kip.edenmatrix.xyz}

cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
sha=$(git rev-parse --short=12 "${ref}^{commit}")
if [ -n "$(git status --porcelain)" ]; then
  echo "note: uncommitted changes are not deployed" >&2
fi

echo "deploying ${sha} to ${host}"
# Unpack beside the current source, then swap, so a failed copy never leaves half a tree.
git archive --format=tar "$sha" | ssh "$host" \
  'set -e; rm -rf /opt/kip/src.new; mkdir /opt/kip/src.new; tar -x -C /opt/kip/src.new;
   rm -rf /opt/kip/src; mv /opt/kip/src.new /opt/kip/src'
ssh "$host" "/opt/kip/src/infra/tunnel/remote-deploy.sh ${sha}"

# Through Cloudflare, after the on-host smoke test passed: a failure here is the tunnel or DNS,
# and the release itself is already running on the host.
if curl -fsS --max-time 20 --retry 5 --retry-delay 3 --retry-all-errors "${url}/health" >/dev/null; then
  echo "public: ${url}/health OK"
else
  echo "public: ${url}/health did not answer; check cloudflared's logs on the host" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Commit messages, house style

Read this before drafting. The failure mode is drifting into an engineering
narrative, and it is easy to do without noticing.

## The flow: draft, confirm, commit, they push

1. **Draft** the message and show it in one plain code block.
2. **Wait.** Never commit on the same turn as the draft. The user is reviewing both
   the message and the commit boundary.
3. **On confirmation**, write the body to `.context/commit-message.txt` (gitignored),
   `git add` only that stage's files, then
   `git commit -F .context/commit-message.txt`.
4. **Stop.** Never `git push`. The user pushes once they agree with what landed.

### Authorship, non-negotiable

The commit is the user's. Their git config supplies the author. Never pass `--author`,
never add `Co-Authored-By`, never add any AI attribution or trailer line of any kind.

### Before committing, mechanically check

    python3 -c "import sys;b=open('.context/commit-message.txt',encoding='utf-8').read();\
    bad=[c for c in b if c in '\u2014\u2013'];print('DASHES:',bad or 'none')"

Any hit, rewrite it. Colons, commas or hyphens instead. Also confirm no `Co-Authored-By`,
no full file paths, and no test counts in the body.

### Scope

One stage per commit. Add that stage's files by name rather than `git add -A`, unless the
user says otherwise. If the subject needs "and also", it should have been two commits.

## Shape

```
<Imperative subject: what the product or system gained>

<Paragraph: what exists now, and honestly what it still does not do.>

<Optional second paragraph: the one decision worth defending, and why.>

- Filename.php: what changed here and why.
- area or filename: what changed here and why.
- tests: what is covered, and how the assertions were proven to have teeth.
```

## The subject line

Imperative, no full stop, names what was added or changed at product level.

Good, taken from real commits in this style:

```
Add the relational policy schema, models and the attention rule
Import legacy governance into relational policies and add the library index
Gate every governance write on canEditWorkspace
Scope policies to the property group
Align policies-v2 docs to company ownership
```

If the subject needs "and also", it should have been two commits.

## The opening paragraph: be additive

This is the part that goes wrong. Lead with **what the system can now do**, and
state plainly what it still cannot. Two real examples:

> First structural phase of the Policies rebuild: the tables exist and are
> unit-testable, and nothing reads them yet, so the change is additive and
> invisible.

> The importer builds each workspace from the real taxonomy and only overlays
> whatever was saved before, because the old data can't be trusted.

Both open with the thing that now exists. Neither opens with the process of
building it.

## Bullets

One per file or area. **Bare filenames or short area names, never full paths.**
Dense prose sentences, not fragments. Reasoning inline, in the same sentence as
the change.

```
- PolicyEventTypeEnum.php: fourteen cases, the single vocabulary behind history
  chips, the Agent Log filter options and the WorkOS action names. Values stay
  inside string(32) so the column does not need widening.
- migrations: policy_events gains uuid, correlation_id and mirrored_at. uuid is
  the event's public identity and the WorkOS idempotency key, so a retried mirror
  cannot duplicate upstream.
```

Group related files under one area bullet (`migrations:`, `tests:`) rather than
listing each.

The last bullet is always `tests:`, covering what is asserted and, where
mutation testing was done, that the assertions fail without the fix.

## Plain words, and few of them

Write for someone skimming `git log`, not for someone admiring the design.

**Cut invented precision.** Phrases that sound exact but carry no meaning to a
reader: "taxonomy positions", "the canonical vocabulary", "the seam", "first-class
records", "the discipline". If a plainer sentence says the same thing, use it.

    no    References are taxonomy positions, not free text
    yes   A new policy is numbered automatically from its category

    no    the write path funnels through a single mutation surface
    yes   all edits go through PolicyWriteService

**Keep bullets to one or two sentences.** If a bullet needs three, either the
change is doing too much or the detail belongs in the code comment instead.

**Say the effect, not the mechanism**, unless the mechanism is the point.

    no    ds-form-control applies text-transform uppercase and the console body
          carries the hq-app class so the cascade reaches it
    yes   dialog fields show what was typed. They were inheriting the HQ form
          style, which forces uppercase.

**Target length.** Subject, a short paragraph, one optional second paragraph, then
one bullet per file. If it runs much past that, cut rather than reorganise.

## Do not

- **Tell the story of finding the bug.** "Two faults surfaced only by driving it",
  "a test caught", "it turned out", "I discovered". The reader wants the state of
  the system, not the diary. If a fault is worth mentioning, say what the code now
  does and why, in one clause.
- **Lead with process.** Not "after the merge I ran the suite and". Lead with the change.
- **Headline test counts.** "195 tests passing" belongs in chat, not the message.
  Numbers that age badly do not belong in permanent history.
- **Use full file paths.** `PolicyWriteService.php`, not
  `app/Services/Policies/PolicyWriteService.php`.
- **Use em-dashes anywhere.** Colons, commas or hyphens instead. This applies to
  every generated artifact, not just commits.
- **Narrate the plan.** No stage numbers, phase names, ticket references or
  "as agreed". The commit records the code, not the schedule.

## Self-check before handing it over

1. Does the first sentence say what the system can now do?
2. Could a reader who was not in the conversation follow it?
3. Is every bullet a change plus its reason, rather than a list of edits?
4. Any discovery narrative left? Cut it.
5. Any em-dash? Any full path? Any test count in the body? Cut them.
6. Would the subject still make sense in a changelog?
